name: Keto diet
lead: The ketogenic (keto) diet is a very low-carbohydrate, high-fat, adequate-protein eating pattern that shifts the body toward burning fat and producing ketone bodies. It began as a medical therapy for drug-resistant epilepsy, mainly in children, in the 1920s and became one of the most widely followed weight-loss diets of the late 2010s. [1][2][5]

For appearance, the diet is used to lose body fat quickly and look leaner: lower body fat shows up as a more defined jawline, more visible cheekbones and a sharper physique, and members of looksmaxxing communities post before-and-after photos and weight-loss reports with that goal. [3][10] Posters describe the scale moving quickly in the first weeks, and reviews note that early loss on low-carbohydrate diets includes water. [10][11]

Reviews describe the weight-loss evidence as mixed. Low-carbohydrate diets can produce more loss than low-fat diets in the short term, but higher-quality meta-analyses find little or no difference over longer periods, and researchers attribute most of the loss to calorie restriction and adherence. Reviews also report a substantial rise in LDL cholesterol in many people, and professional bodies such as the American Heart Association have said the evidence is insufficient to support the diet for heart health. [2][4]

angle.text: The diet is used as a fat-loss method: reducing carbohydrate lowers calorie intake for many people, and lower body fat makes facial structure and muscle definition more visible. Reviews report quick early weight loss that converges with other diets over longer periods. [2][4]

paras: In ketosis the liver converts fatty acids into ketone bodies (acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetone), which the brain and muscles can use when carbohydrate intake is low. A diet that gets most of its energy from fat, moderate protein and very little carbohydrate keeps the body in this state. [6]

The classic medical version uses a 4:1 ratio of fat to combined protein and carbohydrate by weight. The MCT version uses medium-chain triglyceride oil, which permits more carbohydrate and protein. The modified Atkins diet sets no calorie or protein limits and caps carbohydrate at roughly 10 to 20 g a day; the low glycaemic index treatment allows around 40 to 60 g a day from low-glycaemic foods. [1]

Weight-loss versions are defined several ways, including under about 50 g of carbohydrate a day, a very low-calorie ketogenic diet capped at 800 kcal per day, and a modified Atkins approach under 10 g of carbohydrate a day. Organisations draw the line for low-carbohydrate eating differently (for example under 20 percent of calories from carbohydrate for the American Academy of Family Physicians, under 25 percent for the National Lipid Association), which complicates comparison of studies. [2]
Typical foods are meat, fish, eggs, cheese, nuts, oils and leafy or other non-starchy vegetables, while bread, pasta, sugar, rice and starchy vegetables are limited. [2]

The Hippocratic treatise On the Sacred Disease argued around 400 BC that epilepsy had a physical basis open to dietary therapy. A 1911 French study of 20 patients used a low-calorie diet with fasting, and Hugh Conklin's 1920s water diet claimed a high cure rate in children. [1]

The term ketogenic diet is credited to Russell Wilder of the Mayo Clinic, who ran the first epilepsy trial of it in 1921. In 1925 Mynie Peterman reported that 60 percent of 37 children became seizure-free. Use declined after phenytoin was discovered in 1938, and Peter Huttenlocher devised the MCT version in 1971. [1]

Interest returned after Jim Abrahams founded the Charlie Foundation in 1994 following his son's response to the diet, a multicentre study was published in 1998, and the 1997 television film First Do No Harm, starring Meryl Streep, dramatised the story. By 2007 the diet was offered at about 75 centres in 45 countries. [1]

Low-carbohydrate weight loss has a separate lineage. John Rollo reported treating diabetic officers with a low-carbohydrate diet in 1797, and Jean Anthelme Brillat-Savarin promoted a low-carbohydrate approach in 1825. [2]

William Banting, a London undertaker, published Letter on Corpulence, Addressed to the Public in 1863. He reported his weight falling from 202 lb in August 1862 to 156 lb in September 1863 on a plan of meat, greens, fruit and dry wine that avoided sugar, starch, beer, milk and butter. He paid for the first printing himself and gave profits to charity. The pamphlet stayed popular for years, and in English and Swedish the verbs banting and banta came to mean dieting. [12]

Robert Atkins published Dr. Atkins' Diet Revolution in 1972, promising a way to stay thin on a high-calorie diet; the book drew criticism from the American Medical Association, the American Dietetic Association and the American Heart Association, who called it nutritionally unbalanced. Atkins Nutritionals, founded in 1989, filed for Chapter 11 protection in July 2005 after Atkins's death in 2003. [2][11]

Low-carbohydrate diets peaked in the United States in the early 2000s: at the 2003 and 2004 peak, as many as 1 in 11 North American adults said they were following one, and by 2004 the share had fallen to about 2 percent. [11]

Keto returned as a mainstream consumer diet in the late 2010s. A 2022 review reported that with 25.4 million unique searches it was the most Googled diet in the United States in 2020, that the global ketogenic diet market was worth about 9.57 billion US dollars in 2019, and that it had been discussed by celebrities, health magazines and documentaries. [5] In 2018 the British Dietetic Association listed it among its worst celebrity diets, and the American Heart Association said in 2021 that evidence was insufficient to support keto or intermittent fasting for heart health. [2]

Much of the modern low-carbohydrate movement draws on the carbohydrate-insulin hypothesis, which holds that carbohydrates are uniquely fattening because they raise insulin and drive fat storage. Science journalist Gary Taubes popularised it through a 2002 New York Times Magazine article, Good Calories, Bad Calories (2007) and Why We Get Fat (2010). The 2002 article drew strong controversy, and some scholars it quoted said they were misrepresented. [13]

In September 2012 Taubes and Peter Attia founded the Nutrition Science Initiative to test the hypothesis. A 2014 pilot study led by NIH researcher Kevin Hall did not support it, and Hall wrote in 2017 that experiments had falsified it; critics of Taubes, including obesity researcher George Bray, dispute his reading of the evidence, while Taubes and supporters maintain that carbohydrate restriction produces fat loss beyond calorie control. [2][13]

Atkins likewise claimed that the diet burned extra calories, estimating a 950-calorie daily advantage; a Lancet review found no such advantage and concluded that dieters were simply eating less. [11] A 2022 review of ketogenic diets and energy expenditure noted that some researchers have hypothesised a short-term rise in energy expenditure early on, from the work of making glucose and recycling fats, followed by a possible fall later. [6]

Reviews report that low-carbohydrate diets can produce more weight loss than low-fat diets in the short and medium term, with the advantage fading over time. A 2022 Cochrane review found no benefit over balanced diets at two years, and an Endocrine Society statement noted that with calories held constant, body-fat accumulation does not appear to be affected even by pronounced changes in the fat to carbohydrate ratio. A 2017 review concluded that loss is mainly driven by calorie restriction and adherence rather than diet type. [2]

A 2020 review in Atherosclerosis said the diet causes rapid weight loss and favourable changes in markers such as glycated haemoglobin in type 2 diabetes, while also raising LDL cholesterol enough that many physicians hesitate to endorse it, and it noted the popular uptake of keto among people not in need of weight loss. It also pointed out that very few randomized trials of diets have addressed weight loss and cardiovascular outcomes together. [4]

The Atkins diet produced 0.1 to 2.9 percent more weight loss than behavioural counselling at one year in trials summarised on Wikipedia, and the early difference is thought to include substantial water loss. [11] In one cited study a very-low-calorie ketogenic diet produced about 10 kg of average loss over four weeks, and the authors urged medical supervision because of sodium concerns. [2]
Adherence matters in these comparisons: in one study low-carbohydrate dieters adhered well at six months but had the most dropouts by two years. [2]

Low-carbohydrate diets may reduce endurance for high-intensity exercise. [2] A 2025 systematic review of six clinical trials combining a ketogenic diet with endurance training found increased VO2max and reduced body mass in several of them, but the changes were not statistically significant in the pooled comparison because the data were sparse. [14]

The review's authors did not conclude whether such changes are beneficial. For people who train for muscle, the question that proponents and critics debate is whether very low carbohydrate intake supports training volume; no trial in these reviews measured facial or physique appearance directly. [14]

In children on the medical diet, reported effects include constipation, raised blood lipids (affecting up to 60 percent), kidney stones in roughly 1 in 20, slowed growth and fractures. In adults, reported effects include weight loss, constipation, dyslipidaemia and dysmenorrhoea. [1]

For weight-loss versions, constipation, headache, bad breath, muscle cramps and weakness are commonly reported, and rare cases of ketoacidosis and nutrient-deficiency complications have been described. Long-term use can raise total and LDL cholesterol; a 2023 case series described dramatic LDL rises in people following ketogenic diets, and a 2024 letter in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition argued that very low-carbohydrate and keto diets increase unhealthy cholesterol. [2][16][17]

A 2023 study reported that low carbohydrate intake correlated with trends toward insulin resistance and metabolic acidosis in healthy lean individuals. [18] A 2024 laboratory study reported that a ketogenic diet promoted tumor metastasis in mouse models through a BACH1-related mechanism; its relevance to humans has not been established. [7] A 2021 Japanese study linked high adherence to low-carbohydrate eating with higher cancer risk, mainly through animal foods. [2]
A 2026 randomized pilot study reported that a ketogenic diet was less effective than a Mediterranean diet at reducing depression and anxiety in people with obesity. [15]

The American College of Cardiology advises caution for people with atherosclerosis, and the diet is contraindicated in several rare metabolic disorders, including pyruvate carboxylase deficiency, porphyria and fatty-acid oxidation disorders. [1][2] The American Heart Association (2021) said evidence is insufficient to support popular diets such as ketogenic, and the British Dietetic Association listed it among its worst celebrity diets in 2018. [2]

Members of looksmax.org discuss keto as a fat-loss route and post physique photos asking whether they look leaner on it. [3] Posters report rapid scale loss, for example about 5 kg in a month. [10] Some members dispute its value or safety, and others argue that calorie control and food quality matter more than diet type. [8] Threads also discuss cholesterol and whether a high-fat diet affects testosterone. [9]

Keto is typically one option among several cutting strategies discussed alongside calorie counting, intermittent fasting and high-protein eating, and posts tend to centre on how fast leanness shows in the face and abdomen.

Controlled trials of the ketogenic diet exist for epilepsy, where a 2018 Cochrane review of 11 randomized trials found nearly 38 percent of children had half or fewer seizures on the diet, versus 6 percent of controls, and clinical guidelines in the UK recommend it as an adjunct for drug-resistant epilepsy in children. [1] For weight loss, meta-analyses of low-carbohydrate versus low-fat diets are summarised above. [2][4] Trials of a ketogenic diet in athletes and of keto versus a Mediterranean diet on mood are small. [14][15] No studies were found that tested the diet specifically for facial or other appearance outcomes.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org keto appears as one of several fat-loss approaches, with members sharing results, posting physique photos for feedback and arguing over its safety. [3][8]

claims.claim: Keto is the fastest way to lose fat and look leaner.
claims.believers: Posters describe quick scale loss, such as roughly 5 kg in a month, and ask others to judge whether they look leaner after switching. [3][10]
claims.experts: Reviews report that low-carbohydrate diets can give greater short-term loss than low-fat diets, but that the advantage fades and that calorie restriction and adherence drive results. [2][4]

claims.claim: Carbohydrates are uniquely fattening because of insulin, so cutting them cuts fat.
claims.believers: Taubes and other proponents argue that high insulin locks fat in storage and that low-carbohydrate eating works beyond calorie restriction. [13]
claims.experts: Kevin Hall's 2014 pilot study did not support the hypothesis and he wrote in 2017 that experiments had falsified it; reviews attribute most loss to calories and adherence. [2][13]
A Lancet review found no such advantage; a 2022 review described possible early rises and later falls in energy expenditure on ketogenic diets. [6][11]

claims.believers: One thread asks whether this is true or a dismissal by people who dislike the diet, and some replies say it is not bad if protein and calories are managed. [8]
claims.experts: Kidney stones occur in about 1 in 20 children on the medical diet, and high protein intake is a general concern in kidney disease; evidence for healthy adults on weight-loss versions is limited. [1][2]

claims.claim: A high-fat keto diet raises cholesterol and does not raise testosterone.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread argues that raising cholesterol through high-fat eating will not raise testosterone and may contribute to atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. [9]
claims.experts: Long-term low-carbohydrate use can raise total and LDL cholesterol, as shown in case series and reviews; no source reviewed here tested testosterone effects. [2][17]

claims.believers: Proponents say fat adaptation lets athletes lose body mass while keeping performance.
claims.experts: A 2025 systematic review of six trials saw increased VO2max and reduced body mass in some, with no statistically significant pooled result, and low-carbohydrate diets may reduce high-intensity endurance. [2][14]

card.summary: A very low-carb, high-fat diet used for fat loss; trials show short-term loss but little edge over other diets once calories are matched.
card.note: Evidence for appearance is indirect; guidance bodies do not endorse it for heart health.

quick.overview:
The keto diet limits carbohydrate so heavily that the body produces ketones from fat. It began as an epilepsy treatment in the 1920s and became a popular weight-loss diet.

In looksmaxxing circles it is used for leaning out. Reviews find short-term loss greater than low-fat diets, with the gap shrinking over time.
quick.mechanism: With carbohydrate restricted, the liver produces ketone bodies that substitute for glucose. Researchers attribute most weight loss to reduced calorie intake and adherence rather than ketosis itself.
quick.risks: Reported effects include constipation, headache, cramps, raised LDL cholesterol and, in children on the medical diet, kidney stones and slowed growth. Rare ketoacidosis cases exist. The American Heart Association says evidence is insufficient to support it for heart health.
